paper_title: SoftwareGym: Scaling Computer-Use Agent Training with Diverse Synthesized Software Environments

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are rapidly improving, yet synthesizing diverse and reliable software environments at scale remains challenging. Native application environments require substantial construction and integration effort, which limits application coverage and increases the risk of application-specific overfitting. Browser-hosted environments provide limited interaction depth and workflow complexity. These limitations motivate SoftwareGym, an automated pipeline for synthesizing GUI software environments with diverse interfaces, executable functionality, and runtime-verified behavior. It generates structurally diverse designs, realizes them as runnable applications, and uses GUI evaluation with iterative repair to ensure functional reliability. Using SoftwareGym, we synthesize 182 applications across twelve categories and achieve a mean GUI task pass rate of 91.5%. We construct SoftwareGym-Bench, a 120-task evaluation suite spanning the same twelve categories, and use trajectories collected from these environments for CUA training. The resulting model improves Pass@3 from 41.39% to 56.97% on the strictly out-of-domain OSWorld benchmark and achieves 40.0% on SoftwareGym-Bench. These results demonstrate the potential of synthesized software environments as scalable and transferable supervision for CUA training.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Training capable computer-use agents (CUAs) requires interaction data from executable software environments (Qin et al., 2025). To support generalization, these environments must provide diverse, realistic, and reliable trajectories. Constructing such environments at scale has therefore become central bottleneck for CUA training. Current data synthesis either generates tasks and trajectories within existing desktop and mobile applications (Sun et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2026; Jung et al., 2026) or constructs browser-hosted software environments (Cao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). Native applications preserve realistic states and complex workflows, but the cost of integrating them into reproducible training environments limits application coverage and increases the risk of application-specific overfitting. Browser-hosted environments support scalable deployment and state control, but their shared substrate limits interaction depth and workflow complexity. Existing approaches do not jointly satisfy three requirements for CUA training: interface and interaction diversity to support generalization, functional reliability to produce valid, complex trajectories, and scalability to expand the environment pool with limited engineering effort. Achieving these three requirements introduces three corresponding challenges: interface and interaction diversity is difficult because unconstrained generation within the same software category often converges toward similar layouts and interaction patterns; functional reliability 1 arXiv preprint Figure 1: Representative applications synthesized by SoftwareGym. Pic-Editor, VideoPlayer, TableEditor, and CodeEditor represent diverse software categories and GUI designs. Each row traces representative multi-step workflow, demonstrating substantial interaction depth. requires every specified function to remain usable through complete GUI workflows; scalability requires these diversity controls and reliability checks to be applied across large software pool, creating verification burden that manual development cannot sustain. To address these challenges, we design SoftwareGym, an automated multi-agent pipeline for GUI software synthesis. For diversity, SoftwareGym creates category-level functional specifications and variant-specific interface and interaction designs. For reliability, it combines source-level verification with checkpoint-based GUI evaluation and repair; only applications that complete both source-level and GUI verification enter the software library. For scalability, it automates the complete process with minimal human input, enabling applications to be generated in batches with substantially lower time and monetary costs than manual development. To realize these goals, synthesis proceeds in three stages. The design stage expands minimal human input into detailed functional specification, diverse UI blueprints, and corresponding interaction schemes. The implementation stage converts each design package into an executable application and verifies its source-level functionality. The evaluation stage executes checkpoint-based GUI tests and guides iterative implementation repair. These stages enable SoftwareGym to produce diverse and functionally reliable software environments with realistic multi-step workflows at scale. Using this pipeline, we construct large, diverse, and functionally reliable software library in substantially less time and at lower monetary cost than manual development. We synthesize 182 runnable applications across twelve categories, with mean GUI task pass rate of 91.5%. Figure 1 illustrates their functional depth across representative software categories. We use trajectories collected from these applications to train model. Without using any OSWorld applications, tasks, or trajectories for training, it improves Pass@3 from 41.39% to 56.97% on OSWorld, demonstrating strong out-of-domain generalization. For complementary evaluation, we evaluate the model on SoftwareGym-Bench, dedicated 120-task test set spanning the same twelve categories; it achieves 40.0% Pass@3 and outperforms several larger specialized computer-use agents. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We introduce SoftwareGym, an automated environment-synthesis pipeline that produces functionally reliable and structurally diverse software at scale, with substantially lower development time and monetary cost than comparable manually developed applications. (2) We release 182 runnable applications across twelve categories and construct SoftwareGymBench, dedicated 120-task test set spanning the same twelve categories. (3) Through extensive evaluations and ablations, we validate the pipelines key components and show that the model trained only on SoftwareGym trajectories improves OSWorld Pass@3 by 15.58 points to 56.97%. 2 arXiv preprint

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Data Synthesis in Existing Software. Benchmarks such as OSWorld, Windows Agent Arena, and AndroidWorld first make real desktop and mobile applications reproducibly accessible for CUA evaluation (Xie et al., 2024; Bonatti et al., 2024; Rawles et al., 2025). Subsequent work synthesizes tasks and trajectories within existing desktop and mobile applications (Sun et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2026; Jung et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Xue et al., 2026). CUA-Universe and Gym-Anything further adapt and configure existing software as reproducible agent environments (Shi et al., 2026; Aggarwal et al., 2026). Complementary systems refine online traces, collect human demonstrations, or train over decentralized CUA data (Qin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b;a). Although these approaches preserve authentic software states and complex workflows, their coverage remains constrained by the availability and integration cost of existing applications. Repeated training on this fixed software pool may also encourage application-specific overfitting. SoftwareGym instead synthesizes new executable applications with controllable functions, interfaces, and interaction logic, directly expanding the software distribution. Synthesis of Browser-Hosted Software Environments. InfiniteWeb and AutoWebWorld first establish scalable browser-hosted environments through multi-page websites and state-machinegenerated Web worlds (Zhang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). GUI-GENESIS and ScaleWoB further extend this approach toward software interaction by reconstructing real applications or synthesizing software interfaces as backend-free webpages (Cao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). Although these approaches simplify deployment and state control, their shared browser/HTML/DOM substrate limits native application structure and persistent workflows. SoftwareGym instead synthesizes standalone desktop applications.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: Figure 2 summarizes software synthesis in SoftwareGym. Software Design (3.1) specifies application functions and interfaces. Software Implementation and Evaluation (3.2) then realizes each application and iteratively repairs it using failures observed through GUI interaction. Applications that complete this verification loop enter the software library. Task Synthesis (3.3; Figure 3) converts their verified functions into executable GUI tasks.

sections.title: 3.1 SOFTWARE DESIGN
sections.content: The design stage produces rich, realistic functional specifications and specifies diverse GUI structures and interaction patterns for each software variant. Given software type and supporting resources, it produces shared Software Specification and multiple style-specific Verified Design Packages. Each package contains the Software Specification, UI Blueprint, and SVG Assets. Function Design. Function design specifies the purpose of an application and the detailed functions it should provide. Given the Software Type and Resources, FUNCTIONDESIGNER expands the initial description through four-step workflow. First, it establishes the functional baseline of mature product by identifying its target users, core objects, and expected operations, such as creating, opening, editing, organizing, searching, recovering, and saving content. Second, it extends each module with domain-specific professional functions, including multi-condition retrieval, batch operations, history management, persistent view settings, and input validation. Third, it connects these functions into complete user workflows, from creating or opening content to editing, organization, retrieval, and final save or export. The workflows also cover cross-module state changes, dependent operations, failure handling, and recovery. Finally, it records each function in the Software Specification as an implementation and evaluation contract. The contract specifies the user entry, user action, expected state update, visible GUI response, and acceptance checkpoint. These steps provide functional breadth and operational depth while making every function implementable and directly verifiable through GUI interaction. Style Diversification. Given shared functional specification from FUNCTIONDESIGNER, this stage generates multiple diverse, implementation-ready Avalonia UI blueprints. These blueprints realize the same software functionality with different interface and interaction designs. STYLEDESIGNER 3 arXiv preprint Figure 2: SoftwareGym synthesizes diverse, reliable, and executable applications through design, implementation, and evaluation. Design produces rich functional specifications and distinct interfaces. Implementation realizes and verifies the applications. Evaluation tests their GUI behavior and returns failures for subsequent implementation repair. creates distinct style specifications that define different product positions, information architectures, interaction patterns, and visual identities. Each specification follows layout archetype that determines navigation, spatial organization, object browsing, and action placement. To prevent variants from converging to similar interfaces, every pair of variants must differ along at least two layout dimensions. Appendix formally defines this distance. Each style specification is assigned to an independent SUBSTYLEDESIGNER. Each SUBSTYLEDESIGNER converts its specification into concrete screen structures and interaction flows. We compile every generated XAML file to verify that it is valid and executable. To further ensure that the generated variants are structurally different rather than merely cosmetically different, we represent each blueprint as normalized layout tree over windows, regions, panels, and controls. We then compute pairwise tree-edit distance between these trees. If the minimum pairwise distance falls below predefined threshold, we regenerate the least distinct blueprint. Appendix defines the metric and its normalization. These checks ensure that the retained blueprints are executable and structurally distinct. Icon and SVG Asset Generation. ICONDESIGNER derives style-independent Icon Candidate Manifest from the Software Specification, covering application, action, navigation, status, contenttype, entity, avatar, and illustration icons. For each interface variant, SUBSTYLEDESIGNER assigns icon candidates to GUI slots, and SUBICONDESIGNER renders them as style-specific SVG assets. Icons with the same semantic role across variants are required to differ structurally rather than only by color. platform-side validator checks asset completeness, SVG validity, and safety constraints. The resulting icon assets and slot mappings are included in the Verified Design Package. Together, these constraints preserve functional consistency while introducing visual diversity across synthesized software variants.

sections.title: 3.2 SOFTWARE IMPLEMENTATION AND EVALUATION
sections.content: Software Implementation and Evaluation turns each Verified Design Package into runnable application and verifies that it satisfies the specified functional and interface requirements. For each software variant, we implement the application, evaluate its GUI behavior, and use observed failures to guide iterative repair. Application Implementation and Source-Code Verification. CODER uses the Verified Design Package as the implementation specification and realizes the complete Avalonia application, including its structure, visual system, icons, and functionality. Each specified function is implemented as complete GUI workflow, covering user entry points, command bindings, state updates, persistence, and visible feedback. CODER also records each function and its acceptance check in functional manual. DEVCODER then audits the implementation against this manual. It checks command 4 arXiv preprint Figure 3: SoftwareGym grounds every synthesized task in capabilities verified through GUI interaction. It first extracts evidence-supported capabilities, then assigns coherent combinations to difficultyand state-controlled slots, and finally realizes each slot as natural request with an explicit initial state and expected outcome. bindings, application logic, persistence, startup behavior, and file interfaces, and repairs missing or incomplete implementations. In later refinement rounds, CODER and DEVCODER use GUI failure traces and runtime evidence to perform localized repairs while preserving already correct behavior. This process ensures that every specified function is backed by executable logic and produces observable GUI behavior. GUI Test Generation and Evaluation. Source-code verification alone cannot confirm how an application behaves under direct interaction. Evaluation therefore tests the running application independently, covering both functional GUI behavior and visual fidelity to the design package. EVALTASKGENERATEAGENT generates cases from the source-verified functional manual produced during implementation. The cases cover control reachability, navigation, object creation and editing, persistence, retrieval, settings, dialogs, and file workflows. Each case begins from an explicit state, uses only documented functions, and defines visible checkpoints. The case set is fixed after the first implementation and reused across repair rounds. GUIAGENT executes the cases with mouse and keyboard actions and records the interaction trace, checkpoint evidence, final state, failure location, and repair suggestion. Functional pass rate is Pfunc = Npass/Nall, where Npass is the number of passed tasks and Nall is the total number of generated cases. The evaluation report and failed trajectories are returned to implementation for the next repair round. Evaluation stops when all cases pass or the version budget is exhausted. This process grounds implementation repair in reproducible GUI failures and progressively improves functional reliability. Design Fidelity. Functional success alone does not guarantee that repaired application retains its intended interface. Design fidelity therefore ensures that implementation and source-code repair preserve the interface identity of each software variant. After each GUI-evaluation round, SoftwareGym computes normalized visual-fidelity score between the implemented application and its UI blueprint; its calculation is defined in Appendix B. When the score falls below pre-calibrated threshold, the evaluator provides targeted feedback for repair. Structural checks also compare the implemented layout and interface elements with the blueprint. This ensures that implementation repair improves functionality without deviating from the intended interface structure or visual design.

sections.title: 3.3 TASK SYNTHESIS
sections.content: Task synthesis constructs GUI tasks using only application capabilities verified through GUI evaluation. As shown in Figure 3, it consists of three steps: function analysis, difficulty leveling, and task generation. Function Analysis. Function analysis identifies the application capabilities that have been verified through GUI interaction and can be used for task synthesis. It constructs an evidence-grounded function tree for each retained software variant. To build this tree, the pipeline extracts functional manual produced during implementation. It then uses the GUI evaluation report to determine which functions are supported. Each leaf records task-level capability, its support status, GUI entry points, 5 arXiv preprint constraints, observable state, and evaluation evidence. capability is marked supported only when it cites passed case, checkpoint, or interaction step. Untested functions, failed functions, and blocked paths are excluded. This evidence gate prevents task generation from relying on functions that have not been demonstrated in the running application. Difficulty Leveling. Difficulty leveling controls task complexity through dependencies among verified capabilities. Tasks are assigned to three difficulty levels: easy, normal, and hard. Supported capabilities are selected according to the assigned difficulty. An easy task has one primary goal with limited functional composition. normal task combines related objects or operations with necessary dependency between them. hard task forms multi-stage workflow in which each stage establishes state required by the next stage. Each difficulty level contains two task types. file-based task starts with an existing input file. blank-state task starts without an input file and operates from the applications default GUI state. All operations in task must contribute to the same user goal; unrelated or repeated actions cannot be added merely to increase difficulty. These constraints produce comparable difficulty levels while preserving natural, goal-directed workflows. Task Generation. Finally, task generation converts each planned workflow into natural user request and an executable evaluation specification. It checks the selected capabilities against the manual, passed GUI evidence, entry points, state dependencies, persistence behavior, and completion feedback. The request describes one user goal and the constraints required for evaluation. The user-facing request does not expose coordinates, detailed operation paths, capability identifiers, or evaluation mechanisms. The internal task specification records the initial state, outcome criteria, process criteria, and expected final state. Deterministic validation rejects unsupported capabilities, inconsistent initial states, incompatible assets, and unreachable final states. This stage produces natural-language tasks whose requirements remain feasible, observable, and deterministically verifiable.

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Software Synthesis. We synthesize applications across twelve categories using Codex CLI agents with GPT-5.5 for design, implementation, and evaluation-case generation. Each application is refined for up to three versions (v1v3), with the v1 GUI test suite held fixed across rounds and early stopping when all cases pass. Seed 2.1 Pro evaluates each version through mouse-and-keyboard interaction for up to 50 steps per case in isolated virtual machines running Ubuntu 22.04.3 LTS (x86 64). Training. After constructing the software library, we perform multimodal SFT on Qwen3.59B (Team, 2026) using trajectories collected only from SoftwareGym applications. Appendix describes trajectory scoring and filtering, and Appendix C.3 provides the full training configuration. SoftwareGym-Bench. SoftwareGym-Bench is dedicated evaluation suite built on the SoftwareGym application library. We select one application from each of twelve software categories and ten manually verified tasks per application, yielding 120 tasks in total. Each task is constructed to ensure that its target state is reachable and programmatically verifiable. Tasks also include state-grounded distractors and protected objects, requiring agents to reason about which objects to modify, ignore, or preserve rather than simply follow fixed sequence of operations. Further construction details are provided in Appendix A. Evaluation and Baselines. We evaluate the trained model and baselines on OSWorld and SoftwareGym-Bench. OSWorld uses 244 tasks from eight application domains, whereas SoftwareGym-Bench contains the 120 tasks described above. We evaluate GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026b), GPT-5.4 (OpenAI, 2026a), Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 3 Flash (DeepMind, 2026; 2025), Seed 2.0 Pro (Bytedance Seed, 2026a), Seed 2.1 Pro (Bytedance Seed, 2026b), Kimi K2.5 (Team et al., 2026), Qwen3.8-Flash (Qwen Team, 2026b), Qwen3.7-Plus (Qwen Team, 2026a), Qwen3.5 (Team, 2026), Qwen3-VL (Bai et al., 2025), EvoCUA (Xue et al., 2026), DART-GUI (Li et al., 2025), OpenCUA (Wang et al., 2025b), and UI-TARS (Qin et al., 2025). sections.title: 4.2 MAIN RESULT ANALYSIS
sections.content: OSWorld Result Analysis. SoftwareGym-only supervision delivers strong out-of-domain transfer on the eight OSWorld application domains included in our evaluation  (Table 1)  . Without any OSWorld training data, it improves every evaluated domain and raises overall Pass@3 from 41.39% to 56.97%. It remains competitive with much larger open-source baselines across the expanded comparison. This gain shows that reliable and structurally diverse synthesized environments teach transferable GUI 7 arXiv preprint (a) Software distribution (b) Function coverage Figure 4: SoftwareGym scales breadth while preserving runtime-verified functionality. (a) 182 applications span twelve categories. (b) Across 121 applications in eight aligned categories, GUI evidence covers all 49 major modules and 78.8% of concrete native functions. Figure 5: SoftwareGym makes quality-controlled synthesis practical at scale. Bars decompose per-application resource use across design, implementation, and evaluation. (a) GUI pass-rate gains (b) Source-code growth (c) Category-level pass rates Figure 6: Iterative evaluation and implementation repair consistently improve software reliability across the synthesized application library. interaction rather than application-specific procedures, complementing native software by broadening the training distribution. SoftwareGym-Bench Result Analysis. Complementing this out-of-domain result, SoftwareGym supervision supports competitive in-domain learning at compact model scale  (Table 2)  . It substantially improves the same 9B base model, raising Pass@3 by 14.2 points from 25.8% to 40.0%. The resulting model exceeds Qwen3.7-Plus and several substantially larger specialized CUAs. Software Synthesis Analysis. SoftwareGym scales the software library while preserving broad, runtime-verified functionality. Its 182 runnable applications span twelve categories (Figure 4(a)). Among 121 applications from eight categories represented in OSWorld, GUI evaluations cover all 49 major functional modules and 78.8% of concrete functions on average (Figure 4(b)). Appendix defines the evidence criterion. This coverage demonstrates that SoftwareGym expands software breadth while retaining substantial verified functionality. We further characterize synthesis cost by sampling 20 applications. Each application requires 237.3 minutes, 14.8 million tokens, 1,718 model calls, and an estimated $70.76 on average. Figure 5 decomposes these resources across pipeline stages, showing that automated synthesis substantially reduces the cost of constructing software environments at scale. Finally, iterative evaluation and repair improve software reliability across the library. The mean GUI task pass rate increases from 54.9% at v1 to 81.1% at v2 and 91.5% at v3, with consistent gains across categories (Figure 6). sections.title: 4.3 ABLATION STUDIES
sections.content: We next examine the contribution of three key components: structured style design, GUI-guided implementation repair, and the source of training trajectories. Style Design. We compare Full Design with simplified baseline under the same functional requirements and measure structural diversity using normalized tree-edit distance. Full Design improves the macro-average diversity score from 4.9 to 83.6 and achieves higher diversity across all categories (Figure 7(a)). This result shows that explicit style control prevents independently generated designs from collapsing to similar interface structures. Appendix C.1 provides details. Evaluation-Guided Implementation Repair. We compare GUI-guided repair with source-only repair under the same repair process. Starting from the same initial pass rate of 50.4%, GUIguided repair reaches 83.1%, whereas source-only repair ends at 48.8% (Figure 7(b)). This result demonstrates that GUI feedback provides essential runtime evidence for reliable implementation repair. Appendix C.2 provides details. Training Software Source. We compare models trained with trajectories collected from SoftwareGym applications, OSWorld applications, and their combination, while keeping the model and evaluation protocol fixed. The model trained only on SoftwareGym trajectories achieves 56.97% on OSWorld and 40.0% on SoftwareGym-Bench, while combining SoftwareGym and OSWorld trajectories further improves SoftwareGym-Bench performance to 47.5%  (Table 3)  . These results show that synthesized software provides transferable supervision and complements native-software data. Appendix C.3 provides details.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced SoftwareGym, an automated designimplementationevaluation pipeline that synthesizes diverse and functionally reliable desktop applications at scale. Its library contains 182 applications across twelve categories and achieves mean GUI task pass rate of 91.5%; ablations show the value of structured design and evaluation-guided repair. Trajectories collected from these environments provide transferable supervision beyond synthesized software. Without any OSWorld application data for training, it improves Pass@3 from 41.39% to 56.97% on OSWorld and reaches 9 arXiv preprint 40.0% on SoftwareGym-Bench, outperforming several larger specialized agents. SoftwareGym therefore provides rich, scalable complement to native software, broadening the interfaces, interaction patterns, and workflows available for CUA training. 10 arXiv preprint

We construct each task backward from desired final state. We first define the target outcome and then identify the key semantic steps required to reach it. The initial state is built to support these steps and their dependencies. This construction ensures that every task has reachable solution path and well-defined terminal state. State-Grounded Task Difficulty. We introduce distractors and protected objects into the initial state to make task completion require state-grounded decisions. Some objects must be modified, some ignored, and some preserved. The correct action therefore depends on the current application state rather than on fixed sequence of interface operations. This design increases task difficulty while preserving coherent user goal. Programmatic Evaluation. Each task is paired with reproducible initializer and programmatic evaluator. The initializer restores the task to the same initial state before each attempt. The evaluator checks the resulting application state and any produced artifacts against the target outcome. This makes task success deterministically verifiable and results comparable across models and runs. To make the benchmark and its evaluation protocol concrete, we present representative successful trajectories across software categories. sections.content: Layout-Archetype Distance. Layout-archetype distance quantifies how differently two style variants organize interaction at high level. For layout archetypes Li and Lj, we define their distance as the Hamming distance (Hamming, 1950) over navigation, spatial organization, object browsing, and action placement: dlayout(Li, Lj) = (cid:88) 1[ℓi,k = ℓj,k]. k{nav,space,browse,action} Thus, dlayout(Li, Lj) 2 requires the two archetypes to differ in at least two layout dimensions. Enforcing this constraint in SoftwareGym separates style variants before detailed blueprint generation and reduces convergence toward the same interface organization. Structural Blueprint Diversity. Structural blueprint diversity tests whether generated interfaces differ in their component hierarchies rather than only in wording or decoration. We convert each blueprint into normalized layout tree whose nodes represent windows, regions, panels, and interactive controls and whose edges represent containment. Text, colors, fonts, and other visual attributes are removed. Let Ti and Tj be two such trees, and let denote the number of nodes in tree. Using unit costs for node insertion, deletion, and substitution (Zhang & Shasha, 1989), we define (cid:26) (cid:27) dij = min 1, TED(Ti, Tj) max(Ti, Tj) . This gate removes nearduplicate structures and ensures that the retained variants provide meaningfully different interface organizations for implementation. Visual Fidelity. Visual fidelity measures whether an implemented application preserves the design tokens specified by its UI blueprint during iterative repair. Let Cb and Ca denote the sets of color values extracted from the UI blueprint and implemented application, and let Rb and Ra denote their corner-radius sets. We use the Jaccard similarity J(A, B) = B/A B, with J(, ) = 1, and define Fpal = J(Cb, Ca) and Frad = J(Rb, Ra). Fpri and Ffont are binary indicators of whether the blueprints primary color and main font are retained in the application. Fbind = Nres/(Nres+Ninline), where Nres counts resource-based visual references and Ninline counts inline color values; the ratio is set to 1 when its denominator is zero. The primary-color, corner-radius, and font components are set to 1 when the corresponding blueprint property is unspecified. The overall score is Fvis = 0.40Fpal + 0.15Fpri + 0.20Frad + 0.10Ffont + 0.15Fbind. This is design-token implementation gate, not perceptual image-similarity measure. We use pre-calibrated threshold of 0.80, so the gate passes when Fvis 0.80 and the primary color is retained. When an implementation does not satisfy this gate, the evaluator identifies the visual tokens that deviate from the blueprint and returns those mismatches as concrete repair targets. Subsequent repair can therefore correct functional issues without altering the applications intended visual identity. Functional Coverage. Functional coverage measures how comprehensively synthesized applications reproduce the functions available in their corresponding real-world applications. For each synthesized application a, R(2) contains frozen-taxonomy functions verified by at least one passed GUI evaluation case with directly relevant successful checkpoint; claims in the functional manual alone do not count. R(1) contains the parent modules, so level-1 module is cova ered when at least one child function has such evidence. For category and level l, coverage is (l) c,native, where Ac contains the release-selected applications c,native ((cid:83) = (l) )/F (l) R(l) aAc 17 arXiv preprint in category c. Related but insufficient evidence is excluded. We report the unweighted category macro-average as the primary measure and the pooled micro-average as supplementary statistic. We use this measure to verify that expanding the synthesized library preserves broad, directly exercised functionality from corresponding real-world software. 18 arXiv preprint

sections.title: C ABLATION PROTOCOLS AND COMPLETE RESULTS
sections.content: This section separately examines the style-design procedure, the use of GUI feedback during implementation repair, and the software source used to collect training trajectories. Appendix defines the reported metrics, while Appendix details the trajectory filtering used by the training-source ablation. Selections and outputs are frozen in versioned manifests. C.1 STYLE-DESIGN ABLATION The comparison covers Browser, Chat, Code Editor, Forum, Mail, PDF, Rich-text Editor, Image Editor, Slides, Spreadsheet, Music Player, and Video Player. Each method generates one set of ten blueprints per category, yielding 120 Full Design blueprints and 120 Simple Design blueprints (240 total). Both methods receive the same frozen functional requirements and icon inventories. Full Design generates distinct directions and assigns each to an independent designer. It enforces variation in information architecture, layout, visual system, interaction model, and product identity, and rejects structurally redundant designs. Simple Design receives none of these style-control instructions; it is told only that the ten final layouts should differ. Both methods use the same artifact schema and final validators. For each category and method, we average the normalized tree-edit distance over the 45 pairs formed by its ten blueprints, using the same corpus-level structural representation as the production diversity gate. The overall score is the macro-average of the twelve category scores; Appendix defines the tree representation and distance. Full Design produces more diverse blueprint structures in every category and raises the macro-average score from 4.9 to 83.6. Although all Simple blueprints differ at the file level, each category contains at least one pair with the same normalized layout tree, and none of the twelve Simple sets passes the production diversity gate. Table 4: Full Design consistently produces more diverse blueprint structures across all twelve categories. Results are on 0100 scale; each category contains one set of ten blueprints per method.

sections.content: 3.8 2.4 5.7 21.1 4.3 3.4 4.9 C.2 EVALUATION-GUIDED IMPLEMENTATION-REPAIR ABLATION The implementation-repair comparison uses category-balanced paired set of three applications from each of the twelve categories (n = 36), all with complete artifacts from the shared starting checkpoint through both repair rounds. Both branches start from the same v1 source package and use the same two implementation-repair rounds. We run the same GUI evaluation after every round for both branches. In the GUI-guided branch, the resulting report is passed to the Coder for the next repair round; in the source-only branch, the report is recorded but withheld, so the next repair uses source-code evidence alone. Scores average GUI task pass rates over the 36 applications while giving each of the twelve categories equal weight. GUI feedback is decisive: from the shared 50.4% starting score, evaluation-guided repair reaches 70.5% at v2 and 83.1% at v3, while source-only repair reaches 50.5% and then falls below the shared starting score to 48.8%. This regression shows that source-level self-correction alone is insufficient and can even degrade runtime functionality, making feedback from direct GUI testing essential for reliable repair. The final 34.3-point advantage is large and consistent (95% CI: 28.241.0); GUI-guided repair wins on all 36 applications. 19 arXiv preprint Table 5: Evaluation-guided implementation repair substantially improves functional reliability, whereas source-only repair remains near the shared starting level. Before length filtering, the SoftwareGym-only and OSWorld-only datasets are each matched to 3,715 trajectories and 55,263 serialized examples, with identical train/validation/test sizes. Both datasets use the same 0.8 outcome and process thresholds and message-conversion protocol; their post-threshold selection is source-specific, as specified in Appendix E. For the model trained on both sources, we concatenate the complete frozen SoftwareGym-only and OSWorld-only datasets. Because the two datasets are size-matched, each source contributes equally. We preserve their source-prefixed semantic identifiers and original splits, without additional attempt sampling or rewriting. All three models are initialized from Qwen3.5-9B Base and use full-parameter SFT of the language model for one epoch; the visual encoder and merger are frozen. The SoftwareGym-only model is trained with 16 A800 GPUs. The OSWorld-only model and the model trained on both sources are each trained with 8 A800 GPUs. We use bf16, FlashAttention, ZeRO-2, gradient checkpointing, learning rate 5 106, 3% warmup, cosine decay, sequence length 16,384, and micro-batch size 1. Gradient accumulation is 2 for the SoftwareGym-only model and 4 for the OSWorld-only model and the model trained on both sources, keeping the global batch size at 32. Overlength examples are removed rather than truncated, leaving 49,445 examples for SoftwareGym-only training, 49,496 for OSWorld-only training, and 98,941 for training on both sources. Evaluation fixes the context and tool protocol, temperature 1, top-p 0.95, output limit 8,192, 100 interaction steps, and three independent rollouts per task. Tables 6 and 7 give the complete run-level results, while Table 3 summarizes Pass@3 in the main text. Synthesized-software supervision transfers strongly to unseen native applications and complements native-software data. On OSWorld, the SoftwareGym-only model obtains 56.97% Pass@3 without any OSWorld application, task, or trajectory in training, compared with 61.48% for the OSWorldonly model. On SoftwareGym-Bench, the SoftwareGym-only model obtains 40.0%, whereas the OSWorld-only model obtains 33.3%. The model trained on both sources further demonstrates their complementarity, reaching 47.5% on SoftwareGym-Bench while retaining 58.61% on OSWorld. Matching the base model, pre-tokenization corpus size, effective batch size, core optimization settings, and evaluation makes the source of the training trajectories the principal difference between the SoftwareGym-only and OSWorld-only models. sections.title: E TRAJECTORY SCORING AND FILTERING
sections.content: Our trajectory-selection procedure asks two complementary questions: whether the agent reaches the requested final state and whether it follows reliable interaction process. After structural audit, two independent GPT-5.5 judges score each candidate. Qualified trajectories are converted to Qwen3.5 multimodal format, validated, source-specifically selected, and group-split. E.1 TWO-STAGE TRAJECTORY SCORING The outcome and process judges use the following prompts. The user request is the only task specification; generated metadata is not ground truth. Outcome scoring uses up to the final five full assistant messages and their step-aligned post-action screenshots; process scoring uses every full assistant message and up to ten evenly sampled, step-aligned screenshots. We retain an attempt only when both scores are at least 0.8.

sections.title: Prompt for Outcome Scoring
sections.content: System: You are the OUTCOME judge for GUI task. Determine whether the agent truly completed the users request. The user request is the only task specification; ignore any generated planning or explanation metadata. You will receive up to the final five chronological assistant messages. Each message includes the complete available reasoning and assistant content, followed immediately by that exact steps paired post-action screenshot when available. Use message text as context for what the agent attempted, but treat it as an unverified claim; the paired screenshot is the primary evidence of what actually happened. Check the final evidence against every material requirement in the user request. Do not reward an agent merely for declaring success or attempting the right action. Do not evaluate general path efficiency here except where the final messages reveal that the requested result was not actually completed. Score 1.0 for clearly complete evidence, 0.70.9 for completion with only minor deviation, 0.40.6 for substantial partial completion, 0.10.3 for little verified progress, and 0.0 for no relevant verified result. Return only JSON: {"score": "<assessment of actual completion against the user request>"} <0.0-1.0>, "reason": User: # User Request {user request} # Final Five Assistant Messages (chronological; paired screenshots follow their exact messages) {evidence}

sections.title: Prompt for Process Scoring
sections.content: System: You are the PROCESS judge for GUI task. Judge whether the chronological GUI trajectory sensibly, safely, and efficiently pursues the users request. The user request is the only task specification; ignore generated planning or explanation metadata. You will receive every chronological assistant message with its complete available reasoning and assistant content. Up to ten evenly sampled post-action screenshots are inserted immediately after the exact messages that produced them. Accept equivalent GUI paths. Consider coherence, efficiency, error recovery, and unrelated or destructive actions. Explicitly penalize looping, revisiting the same state without progress, and repeatedly attempting the same or equivalent action without meaningful change in strategy. Do not penalize limited retry when it is part of sensible error recovery and the agent adapts based on new evidence. Return only JSON: {"score": "<brief trajectory-quality assessment against the user request>"} <0.0-1.0>, "reason": User: # User Request {user request} # Complete Chronological Assistant Messages {evidence} 26 arXiv preprint E.2 MESSAGE CONVERSION, SELECTION, AND SPLITTING Data from OSWorld and SoftwareGym undergo source-specific selection. For OSWorld, we retain the highest-scoring qualified attempt from each task directory; all score-qualified SoftwareGym attempts proceed to conversion. Selected trajectories from both sources are converted from the teacher schema to Qwen3.5 multimodal format. Attempts failing strict message-format or consistency validation are excluded. After conversion, SoftwareGym caps each frozen semantic group at two trajectories; OSWorld balances eight domains and difficulty to match corpus and split sizes. Both use approximately 90/5/5 group-constrained splits without frozen-group overlap, guarantee relative to the pipelines grouping definition.
